proposition: For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, the sum of k^1 for k = 1..n equals n(n+1)/2.
hypotheses: the sum is empty for n = 0

argument.text: For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, (n-4)*(n^2) equals (n-4)*((n^2) + [n = 4]).
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, at least one of the following holds: n mod 2 = 0; n mod 2 = 1.
There is a integer n with 1 <= n <= 30 for which n^3 > 7.
At n = 1, the sum of k^1 for k = 1..n = 1.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, n^2 + n is congruent to (n^2 + n) + 437 modulo 19.
For every integer n with 2 <= n <= 30, n^2 is at least 2*n.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, n^2 + n is congruent to (n^2 + n) + 247 modulo 19.
There is a integer n with 1 <= n <= 30 for which n^2 > 15.
For every integer n with 2 <= n <= 30, n^3 is at least 3*n.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, (n-3)*(n^2) equals (n-3)*((n^2) + [n = 3]).
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, at least one of the following holds: n mod 2 = 0; n mod 2 = 1.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, (n-3)*(n*(n+1)/2) equals (n-3)*((n*(n+1)/2) + [n = 3]).
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 29, ((n+1)*((n+1)+1)/2) - (n*(n+1)/2) equals (n+1)^1.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, if n mod 4 = 0 then (n*(n+1)/2) mod 2 = 0.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 30, if n mod 2 = 1 then (n^2) mod 2 = 1.
The steps above establish the statement up to 30, and it is taken to hold for the whole range up to 30.
